title: Uniqueness of stable modifications over a normal integral base
statement: Let $T$ be a normal integral quasi-compact quasi-separated scheme [def-pc-integral-scheme], where normal means every local ring is an integrally closed domain, and let $(X,D)$ be a multipointed $T$-curve with smooth generic curve and etale generic marking. For any two stable $\eta$-modifications $f_i:(Y_i,E_i)\to(X,D)$ there is a unique isomorphism of pairs $\alpha:(Y_1,E_1)\xrightarrow{\sim}(Y_2,E_2)$ with $f_2\alpha=f_1$. The isomorphism is the identity on the generic pair under the given generic identifications. A multipointed curve $(X,D)$ over a scheme $T$ means flat [def-weil-flat-morphism] finitely presented [def-sbc-locally-finite-presentation] morphisms $X\to T$, $D\to T$ of pure relative dimensions $1$, $0$ and a closed immersion $D\hookrightarrow X$ [def-weil-closed-immersion]; $D$ may be empty and $X$ need not be separated or proper over $T$. It is semistable if every singular point of every geometric fibre has completed local ring $\Omega[[u,v]]/(uv)$ over its algebraically closed residue field, $D\to T$ is etale [def-weil-etale-morphism], and $D$ lies in the relative smooth locus [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms]. For integral $T$ with generic point $\eta$, an $\eta$-modification of multipointed curves is a compatible pair $f_X:X'\to X$, $f_D:D'\to D$ of proper morphisms [def-weil-proper-morphism], each an isomorphism over a schematically dense open and on its generic fibre. A semistable such modification is stable if in each geometric fibre there is no irreducible component isomorphic to $\mathbf P^1$ that is contracted by $f_X$ and meets the union of the marking and the singular points of $X'$ in at most two points. Geometric fibres are [def-weil-geometric-fibre]; dimension is topological Krull dimension [def-kun-topological-krull-dimension]; the local completion is at the maximal ideal [def-weil-pbc-adic-completion], and $\Omega[[u,v]]$ denotes the two-variable formal power series ring [def-weil-pbc-multivariate-power-series]. Here an open immersion $j:U\hookrightarrow Z$ is schematically dense when $\mathcal O_Z\to j_*\mathcal O_U$ is injective.

source.place: Theorem 1.2, Corollary 1.3(i), and their proof in §5, pp. 35--36; the valuation comparison is Proposition 4.5.1 and global domination is Proposition 5.2. Normality is essential.

proof.text: First record uniqueness of any curve comparison over $X$. On an affine open $\operatorname{Spec}A$ of the integral base, every affine chart $\operatorname{Spec}B$ of the flat source has $B\hookrightarrow B\otimes_A\operatorname{Frac}(A)$: apply [lem-sc-flat-invertible-sections-torsion-free] with the invertible module $\mathcal O$ on each chart to see that multiplication by each nonzero element of $A$ is injective. If two $X$-morphisms from this source to $Y_i$ agree on the generic fibre, their equalizer is closed because $f_i$ is separated, by [def-weil-proper-morphism]. Its ideal restricts to zero in those generic localizations, hence is zero. Thus the morphisms agree. The same argument applies to the flat markings with proper target over $D$. Work over affine opens of $T$ for existence; the comparisons obtained there will agree on overlaps by this argument. No separatedness over $T$ is being assumed.

source.place: Theorem 1.2 and Corollary 1.3(i): uniqueness and locality of the comparison; expanded closed-diagonal argument.

proof.text: On an affine open of $T$, apply [lem-trf-stable-curve-diagram-noetherian-model] with $J=J_{\mathrm{st}}=\{1,2\}$. This gives a dominant map to a normal integral affine scheme $T_0$ of finite type over $\mathbf Z$, a pair $(X_0,D_0)$ and stable modifications $f_{i,0}:(Y_{i,0},E_{i,0})\to(X_0,D_0)$ whose diagram pulls back to the original one. Their generic identifications, flatness, semistability, properness and stability are all part of that node, and all total spaces are reduced. It suffices to construct inverse comparisons for this diagram and then pull them back. In the next three steps write $T,X,Y_i,E_i,f_i$ for this finite-type diagram.

source.place: Proof of Theorem 1.2, first paragraph, printed p. 35; §3.1 and Lemma 5.1(ii).

proof.text: Apply [lem-trf-geometrically-reduced-eta-normal] to each $Y_i\to T$. Its hypotheses hold because $T$ is normal and integral and $Y_i$ is the curve of a semistable multipointed pair. Consequently each $Y_i$ is $\eta$-normal. This is partial normality relative to the generic fibre; no normality of the nodal geometric fibres is asserted.

source.place: Proposition 3.5.2 and proof of Theorem 1.2, printed pp. 20--21, 35.

proof.text: Consider any finite-height valuation ring $V$ of $K=k(T)$ centred on $T$ with the prescribed generic map. By [lem-trf-semistable-marked-base-change], the pulled-back pairs are multipointed, the source pairs remain semistable and the geometric stability conditions persist. Their pair maps remain proper by [lem-weil-pbc-proper-fp-permanence](b) and are generic isomorphisms. They are indeed modifications: [lem-trf-stable-curve-diagram-noetherian-model] supplies a dense open of $T$ over whose preimage both pair maps are isomorphisms before this base change. Its inverse image in $\operatorname{Spec}V$ contains the generic point. Flatness over the domain $V$ makes the preimages of that open schematically dense by the injectivity argument of Step 1. Apply [lem-trf-valuation-semistable-dominates-stable] first with $f_2$ stable and $f_1$ semistable, then with their roles reversed. This gives $Y_{1,V}\to Y_{2,V}$ and $Y_{2,V}\to Y_{1,V}$ over $X_V$. The valuation comparison node explicitly permits the fraction field $K$, without assuming it separably closed.

source.place: Proposition 4.5.1, uniqueness part, and the valuation comparison in the proof of Theorem 1.2, printed pp. 33, 35.

proof.text: Apply [lem-trf-valuative-domination-eta-normal] to $C=X$, with $(a,b)=(f_2,f_1)$, and then with $(a,b)=(f_1,f_2)$. The base is integral of finite type over $\mathbf Z$; all three curve schemes are reduced, flat and of finite type by Step 2; the maps are $\eta$-modifications. Step 3 supplies $\eta$-normality of the source in each application, and Step 4 supplies the comparisons for every finite-height centred valuation ring required by this criterion. Obtain curve morphisms $g:Y_1\to Y_2$ and $h:Y_2\to Y_1$ over $X$ with their prescribed generic identifications. Step 1 gives $hg=1$ and $gh=1$, since both composites have the same generic fibre as the identity. Therefore $g$ is an isomorphism of curves over $X$.

source.place: Proposition 5.2, proof of Theorem 1.2, and proof of Corollary 1.3(i), printed pp. 34--35.

proof.text: The curve isomorphism preserves the markings scheme-theoretically. Restrict $g$ to $E_1$. The ideal of $E_2\hookrightarrow Y_2$ pulls back to an ideal with zero image on $(E_1)_\eta$, since the generic maps are the prescribed maps of pairs. On affine charts of $E_1$, flatness over the integral base embeds the chart ring into its generic localization ([lem-sc-flat-invertible-sections-torsion-free] with the structure sheaf, as in Step 1), so this ideal has zero image already on $E_1$. The quotient-ring description of a closed immersion therefore gives a factorization $g_E:E_1\to E_2$. Its composite to $D$ agrees with $f_{1,D}$: the two maps have the same composite to $X$, and $D\hookrightarrow X$ is a closed immersion and hence a monomorphism. Apply the same argument to $h$. The composites on markings are identities because they become identities after the closed immersions into the curves. This yields an isomorphism of pairs over $(X,D)$. Pull back the finite-type comparisons to each affine open of the original $T$. They agree on overlaps by Step 1 and therefore glue: the continuous maps and the maps of structure sheaves agree locally. Uniqueness follows again from Step 1, and the generic pair map is the identity under the given identifications.

source.place: Corollary 1.3(i), proof on printed p. 35; the marking and open-gluing arguments are written out.

(5) The domination node's hypotheses and its valuation quantifier match exactly; Step 1 then gives gh=1 and hg=1. (6) The markings factor by the ideal argument and the monomorphism, and the affine pieces glue by Step 1. lean.statement: theorem stableModificationUniquenessNormal {T : Scheme.{u}} [IsIntegral T] [CompactSpace T] [QuasiSeparatedSpace T] (hT : ∀ x : T, IsDomain (T.presheaf.stalk x) ∧ IsIntegrallyClosed (T.presheaf.stalk x)) (C : MultipointedCurve T) (hX : Smooth (pullback.snd C.x T.fromSpecFunctionField)) (hD : Etale (pullback.snd C.d T.fromSpecFunctionField)) {C₁ C₂ : MultipointedCurve T} (f₁ : C₁.Hom C) (f₂ : C₂.Hom C) (hf₁ : f₁.IsStable T.fromSpecFunctionField) (hf₂ : f₂.IsStable T.fromSpecFunctionField) : ∃! α : (C₁.X ≅ C₂.X) × (C₁.D ≅ C₂.D), α.2.hom ≫ C₂.i = C₁.i ≫ α.1.hom ∧ α.1.hom ≫ f₂.curve = f₁.curve ∧ α.2.hom ≫ f₂.marking = f₁.marking
